svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon ECS GPU sharing with NVIDIA MPS allocates memory as a required hard ceiling that also drives placement, and compute as an optional ceiling that the scheduler ignores. Amazon ECS places tasks based on GPU memory only and does not account for compute when making placement decisions. All containers on a GPU share the same CUDA context, so a fatal GPU error in one container can affect the others sharing that physical GPU, though containers on other GPUs in the same instance are not affected. The memory ceiling is hard for a single-process container and advisory for a multi-process one, since multi-process applications can consume more GPU memory than configured.
svg.title: Memory decides placement; compute is a ceiling the scheduler never sees
svg.text: It packs by memory and shares everything else.
Amazon ECS GPU sharing with NVIDIA MPS — multiple tasks on one GPU, without application changes.
memory — required, and the only input
“a hard ceiling on the GPU memory that the
container can use”
ECS adds up the memory of all GPU containers in a
task and finds one GPU with enough free.
Hard for one process per container. Advisory otherwise.
maxComputePercent — optional, invisible
“a ceiling on the container’s GPU compute usage,
not a reservation”
Unset → the container can use up to 100 percent.
Idle compute goes to whoever asks for it.
An integer from 1 to 100, and the scheduler ignores it.
The placement rule, stated in one sentence
“Amazon ECS places tasks based on GPU memory only, so it doesn’t account for compute when making
placement decisions.”
So two containers that each want most of the card will be co-located, provided their memory fits.
The fault domain is exactly one physical GPU
“MPS is software-level sharing and all containers on a GPU share the same CUDA context”
“If one container triggers a fatal GPU error … the containers sharing that physical GPU could be affected.
Containers on other GPUs on the same instance aren’t affected.”
A precise boundary: group by criticality per GPU, not per instance.
And the operational burden depends on which capacity type you are on.
On ECS Managed Instances, ECS “monitors the MPS control daemon” and replaces the instance if it becomes
unhealthy. The announcement describes that for Managed Instances only — on ECS on EC2 the daemon is yours.
NOT SUPPORTED AWS Fargate · ECS Express Mode · ECS managed daemon tasks · EXTERNAL (ECS Anywhere)
FLOORS container agent 1.107.0+ · ECS AL2023 GPU-optimized AMI 20261019+
Not recommended for large model training needing the full GPU, or workloads requiring hardware-level isolation.
